tf-01.title: Stage and Screen
explain: **Theater** is an art form in which actors show a story to an audience in the same time and the same space. **Film** is an art form that shows a story on screen by joining together scenes recorded with a camera. The two arts both deal with stories, but they differ in how the audience encounters the story. The works, companies, and characters that appear in this lesson are all fictional, invented to help understanding.

In a theater, the audience's seats are fixed. From its seat, the audience sees the whole stage and chooses for itself where to look. The performance happens live at that moment, so even the same production differs slightly from night to night. A film, once shot and edited, shows the same images every time it is screened.

explain.alt: A picture divided into two panels. In the left panel, labeled Theater (stage), a single stick figure stands on the stage, and lines from the audience markers at the lower edge reach the corners of the stage; the audience sees the whole stage from the same seat. In the right panel, labeled Film (screen), three scene boxes marked ①, ②, and ③ are linked by arrows, and the text says that the scenes chosen by the camera follow one another in order.
explain.caption: How stage and screen show a story to the audience

explain: In a film, the camera decides what to show. It can show only a character's eyes in close detail, or pull back to a distant landscape. The fact that **the maker of the film can decide where the viewer looks** is a major feature of film. By contrast, theater fills a limited space with the actor's body, voice, lighting, and props, and lets the audience complete the scene in their imagination.

The two arts also use different materials.
- Theater: the actors' bodies and voices, stage sets, lighting, and sound are used together, live, in the same place.
- Film: images, sound, and editing are made separately and then combined into one.
The starting point of this course is not to judge which is better, but to compare how each art tells the same kind of story in a different way.

examples.title: Fictional story 'Bus Stop in the Rain'
body: Imagine two people standing silently at a bus stop in the rain. In a theater, one could place two chairs and an umbrella on the stage and have the actors sit apart, showing their awkwardness through the empty space between them. The audience sees that empty space directly.

In a film, one could show the wet shoes of the two people up close, and then show a face glancing sideways. The same awkwardness is conveyed through space in theater and through the scenes chosen by the camera in film.

tf-02.title: Story Structure
explain: People who make stories often think of a story as divided into a few blocks. One widely used framework is the **three-act structure**. This structure is not a rule but a tool for organizing a story. Not every work follows this framework.

The three-act structure divides a story into three parts.
- **Act 1 (setup)**: Shows who the characters are and what their situation is. The event that sets the story in motion happens at the end.
- **Act 2 (confrontation)**: The character tries to achieve what they want but runs into obstacles. It is the longest part.
- **Act 3 (resolution)**: After tension reaches its highest point, the problem is solved or the story reaches its ending.

explain.alt: Three boxes in a row are labeled Act 1 (setup), Act 2 (confrontation), and Act 3 (resolution). Above them, a single line starts at the lower left, rises through Act 2, reaches its highest point near the beginning of Act 3, and then comes down. Below, the text says that the higher the line, the higher the tension.
explain.caption: The three-act structure and the rise and fall of tension

explain: The force that moves a story forward is **conflict**. Conflict is the state in which what a character wants and the thing that blocks it face each other. The blocking force can be another character, the environment, or the character's own fear. Without conflict, the audience has a hard time understanding why the next scene matters.

As in the line in the figure, tension usually builds in Act 2, reaches its highest point near the beginning of Act 3, and is then released. The point where tension is highest is often called the **climax**.

examples.title: Fictional story 'Summer Contest'
body: Soeun wants to sing the solo in her school choir contest (desire). In Act 1, we learn what kind of child Soeun is, that the contest is coming soon, and an audition notice for the solo is posted.

In Act 2, Soeun practices, but her voice becomes hoarse, and a friend is aiming for the same spot. In Act 3, Soeun stands on the stage and realizes what she has gained, regardless of the result. The conflict that drives the whole story is between Soeun's desire and the many difficulties that stand in its way.

tf-03.title: Scene Composition and Shot Size
explain: In film, the continuous image from the moment a camera starts recording until it stops is called a **shot**. Shots are classified by size according to how much of the frame they contain. Depending on the size, the feeling the audience receives and the information they get differ.

explain.alt: Three frames are shown side by side. In frame 1, labeled long shot, a small stick figure appears in full, with a door in the background. In frame 2, labeled medium shot, a large figure from the waist up is visible. In frame 3, labeled close-up, only a face with eyes and mouth fills the frame. Below, the text says that the range contained in the frame becomes narrower from left to right.
explain.caption: Three shot sizes

explain:
- **Long shot**: The whole figure and the surrounding space are shown together. Used to show where a character is and what the surroundings are like.
- **Medium shot**: Roughly the upper body, from the waist up, is visible. Widely used to show conversation or gestures.
- **Close-up**: A small part, such as a face, fills the frame. Gathers the audience's attention on an expression or a small object.

There is no single correct shot size. The same character saying the same line may look lonely in a long shot, together with the surroundings, or may feel closer and more intimate in a close-up. Choose according to what the audience needs to know at this point in the story.
When composing a scene, one usually first shows the place with a long shot and then shows the character with a closer shot. This order is not a fixed law either, but a commonly used method.

examples.title: Fictional story 'Empty Library'
body: Bookshelves stand in rows inside a library, and a small figure sits in one corner. Because this shot shows the whole figure together with the space, it is a long shot, so the emptiness of the library and the figure's loneliness are felt together.
If the shot then cuts to a close-up of the person's face as they open a book and stop, the audience becomes curious about what the figure has discovered.

tf-04.title: Editing
explain: Choosing shots that were filmed and joining them together in sequence is **editing**. The point where one shot changes to another is called a **cut**. When joining shots, which shot to choose, in what order, and for how long to show it are all choices.

explain.alt: Three boxes are linked by arrows. Cut A shows a standing person, and Cut B shows a closed door; the box on the right is labeled a person hesitating in front of a door. Below, the text says that the meaning the audience makes changes depending on the order and pairing of the same cuts, and there is a mark indicating that this is a fictional scene.
explain.caption: Joining Cut A and Cut B creates a new meaning

explain: Each shot has a meaning of its own. But when two shots are joined, the audience works out the relationship between them on its own. If a closed door follows a standing person, the audience may feel that the person is hesitating in front of the door. Meaning that is not directly in either shot arises from joining them.

Editing also determines the pace and feeling of the story. Short shots joined quickly tend to feel hurried or tense, while long shots joined slowly tend to feel relaxed or heavy. This too is not a fixed rule, but a common tendency.
Changing the order of shots can change the story. A smiling face followed by a dark room, and a dark room followed by a smiling face, can give the audience different feelings.

examples.title: Fictional story 'Parcel Box'
body: Cut 1 is a shot of a parcel box placed at the front door, and Cut 2 is a shot of a person looking outside from a window. Joined in this order, it feels as if the person is looking at the box.

If the order is reversed, showing the box after the person at the window, it may feel as though the person had been waiting for the box. The shots stay the same, but the order in which they are joined changes the meaning.

tf-05.title: Acting and Direction
explain: The work of an actor taking on a character and showing it through body and voice is **acting**. **Direction** is the work of guiding how the whole scene is seen and heard. The person who directs is the director. The director sets the course so that the story, the actors, the shots, and the sound work well together.

The first thing an actor asks about a character is the character's **motive**. A motive is the reason the character takes this action now, in other words, what the character wants. When the motive is clear, a gesture becomes an action with a reason, even without dialogue.

explain.alt: Three boxes stacked vertically are linked by arrows from top to bottom. The first says the desire: not wanting to miss the train. The second says the obstacle: the bag is heavy, so the steps are slow. The third says the gesture and action: pulling the bag while running and glancing at a clock.
explain.caption: The link between desire, obstacle, and gesture

explain: As in the figure, there is a desire, there is something that blocks it, and gestures and actions arise between them. This structure is the same as the conflict discussed earlier. A character's gesture can be seen as conflict made visible in the body.

A **gesture** is expression that is not words, such as hands, steps, gaze, or breath. The same line changes its meaning depending on the gesture that accompanies it. Saying "I'm okay" with a smile and saying it with the head bowed sound different from each other.

Direction supports this acting with shots and sound. Deciding whether to show the gaze in a close-up or the steps in a long shot is the work of direction. Acting and direction do not work separately; they make the scene together.

examples.title: Fictional story 'Last Train'
body: Haeun wants to catch the last train (desire). Her bag is heavy, so her steps are slow (obstacle). Haeun runs while pulling the bag and glances at the clock (gesture and action).
Direction can show Haeun's feet and the clock in a close-up, or show Haeun running in the distance in a long shot. Either way, Haeun's motive must be clear for the audience to understand the urgency.

tf-06.title: Drawing a Storyboard
explain: A **storyboard** is a plan that draws a scene panel by panel before it becomes moving images. One panel is one shot, and beneath each panel you write the shot size, the sound, and the dialogue. What matters is deciding which shots to use and in what order, not drawing skill.

explain.alt: Three panels side by side are labeled Panel 1, Panel 2, and Panel 3. Under each panel is a blank line for the shot size and for the sound and dialogue. Below, the text says that one panel is one shot, that stick figures and boxes are enough for the drawing, and that the shot size and sound are written under each panel.
explain.caption: Frame of a three-panel storyboard

explain:
When making a storyboard, write down what you have learned earlier, in order.
1. Decide, in one sentence each, what the character wants (motive) and what blocks it.
2. Divide the scene into a beginning, a middle, and an end (a small version of the three-act structure).
3. Choose a shot size for each panel. Use a long shot for a panel that shows the place, and a close-up for a panel where the expression matters.
4. Read aloud what meaning arises when the panels are joined.
Stick figures and boxes are enough. Even if the drawing is rough, it can serve as a storyboard as long as the shot sizes and their order are visible.

body: Panel 1 (long shot): Two stick figures stand far apart at a bus stop in the rain. Panel 2 (medium shot): One person stops while opening an umbrella. Panel 3 (close-up): A hand holds out the handle of the umbrella toward the other person.

Joined together, the three panels first show the place, then show hesitation, and end with the action of offering something. The motive is the wish to come closer to the other person, and what blocks it is shyness.

tf-07.title: Dramaturgy: Aristotle's <Poetics> and the Principle of Plot
explain: The origin of the narrative theory of all dramatic arts (plays, screenplays, and drama) is <Poetics>, written by Aristotle in the fourth century BCE. Aristotle defined drama and tragedy as an 'imitation of action' (mimesis of action), and among the six elements that make up tragedy he declared **plot (Mythos)** to be 'the soul of tragedy and its first principle.'

The hierarchy of the six elements in <Poetics> is as follows: **plot (the arrangement of events) > character > thought (theme) > diction (spoken language) > melody (music) > spectacle (visual staging)**. Aristotle held that however attractive a character's personality may be, a tragedy cannot stand if the causal arrangement of events (plot) is loose. Characters exist for the sake of action, and the necessary chain of actions is itself the plot.

The key mechanisms that determine the completeness of a plot are **recognition** (Anagnorisis) and **reversal** (Peripeteia). As in Sophocles's <Oedipus Rex>, the greatest tragic thrill is born when the moment the protagonist realizes a fatal truth they had been ignorant of (recognition) and the moment fortune plunges into the opposite abyss (reversal) coincide in one place.

As the events unfold, the audience feels **pity** (eleos) and **fear** (phobos) for the protagonist's downfall, and finally reaches **catharsis** (katharsis), the purging and release of the built-up emotion. Catharsis is not simply weeping; it is a process of spiritual healing and purification in which one rationally perceives the harshness of human fate and the sublimity of existence.

Limitation: Aristotle's theory of plot assumes a thoroughly 'closed narrative in which cause and effect mesh like gears.' However, twentieth-century theater of the absurd (Samuel Beckett's <Waiting for Godot>) and modern multilayered narrative films deliberately break causality, exposing chance and meaninglessness, and thereby go beyond the traditional rules of the Poetics.

examples.title: Combining 'recognition and reversal' in Oedipus the King
body: Condition: Oedipus pursues the murderer of the former king Laius in order to resolve the plague in Thebes.
Step 1: Through a messenger's testimony, he realizes that he is the son of Laius, the very man he killed, and that he has married his own mother (recognition).
Step 2: Fortune drops vertically, from a king who saved the city to a cursed transgressor overnight (reversal).
Interpretation: Recognition and reversal combine into a single causal event and release an extreme catharsis.

examples.title: Causal analysis of plot and character
body: Condition: A description of a character as good alone does not make a drama.
Step 1: The good character must be shown, through events, deciding and acting in a desperate crisis.
Step 2: The result of that action must set off a new crisis, forming a causal chain.
Interpretation: Character is truly proven only through action and plot, not through lines of dialogue.

tf-08.title: Dramaturgy: Syd Field's Three-Act Paradigm and the Eight-Sequence Structure
explain: The golden formula of popular narrative that holds the audience's attention for about 120 minutes, from Hollywood commercial films to contemporary well-made series, is the **three-act structure**. The American screenwriter Syd Field systematized it as a 'screenplay paradigm,' and Frank Daniel further subdivided it into eight sequences.

The time allocation and turning points (plot points) of the three-act structure:
- **Act 1: Setup (about 30 minutes, 25% of the whole)**
  - **Ordinary world**: Shows the protagonist's lack and the status quo.
  - **Inciting incident** (about 10 to 15 minutes): A decisive event that breaks the protagonist's calm occurs, and a goal is given.
  - **Plot Point 1** (about 25 to 30 minutes): The protagonist makes a decision and enters a new world from which there is no return, the 'Rubicon.'
- **Act 2: Confrontation (about 60 minutes, 50% of the whole)**
  - The protagonist moves toward the goal and meets increasingly strong obstacles.
  - **Midpoint** (about 60 minutes): At the exact center of Act 2, the protagonist experiences a false victory or a false defeat, the balance of the narrative is completely overturned, and the protagonist shifts from passive response to active attack.
  - **Plot Point 2** (about 85 to 90 minutes): The moment of despair in which all of the protagonist's plans collapse, 'All Is Lost' (the dark night of the soul).
- **Act 3: Resolution (about 30 minutes, 25% of the whole)**
  - **Climax**: The protagonist overcomes their inner flaw and fights a final decisive battle with the antagonist.
  - **Resolution / denouement**: A new order is restored, and the protagonist's changed self is revealed.

The eight-sequence model splits Act 1 into 2 sequences, Act 2 into 4 sequences, and Act 3 into 2 sequences, and places a mini-climax and a dramatic question about every 15 minutes, so that the audience has no time to get bored.

Limitation: The three-act structure guarantees strong commercial appeal, but it risks degenerating into standardized clichés. European art-house films and contemporary Korean films (for example, those by Bong Joon-ho and Lee Chang-dong) secure originality by deliberately disrupting the predictable timing of the three acts or by leaving the ending open.

tf-09.title: Dramaturgy: A Character's Super-Objective and Subtext
explain: A living character who makes the audience laugh and cry does not come from plausible settings (appearance, occupation, age). A character's vitality bursts forth only from **'What does this character crave?'** (desire) and **'What price does the character pay in the face of obstacles that block that desire?'** (conflict).

1. **Super-objective and Want vs. Need**:
- **Super-objective**: The ultimate craving that runs through the whole play and keeps the character moving to the end (a concept of Stanislavski).
- **External desire (Want)**: The concrete goal the character consciously wants and says aloud (for example, "I will earn money," "I will catch the culprit").
- **Internal need (Need)**: A lack or moral flaw that the character does not know about but must fill in order to be truly redeemed (for example, "learning to trust and love other people").
The protagonists of great films usually pursue an external goal (Want) and are frustrated, and eventually realize an internal lack (Need) and achieve personal growth.

2. **Subtext**:
The surface lines spoken by the actor (text), together with the character's real emotions, hidden motives, and secret intentions behind those lines, are called **subtext**. In real life, too, people seldom say what matters most directly. The subtext of the line "Have you eaten yet?" may be "I want to make up," "I am worried about you," or "Please leave now." The greater the gap between the spoken words and the underlying meaning, the more three-dimensional the line becomes and the deeper the suspense.

3. **Beats and power dynamics**:
A scene that stays static is a dead scene. The smallest unit of action in which the psychological superiority (power) between characters shifts within a scene is called a **beat**. When A attacks and B defends, and then B counterattacks successfully by exposing a hidden secret, one beat turns. Each time a beat changes, the character's strategy (tactic) changes.

Limitation: If the subtext is too obscure or overly tangled, the audience cannot follow the character's motives and gets lost. A good playwright must subtly leave hints through visible action and symbolic mise-en-scène, so that the audience can decode the subtext.

examples.title: Three-dimensional design of lines and subtext
body: Situation: A married couple on the verge of divorce sit facing each other at the dinner table.
Surface line (text): "Pass me the salt. The soup is so bland."
Subtext: "The ten years of our married life together have been as bland and tasteless as this soup. I am sick of it now."
Interpretation: Through an everyday object (the salt), deep resentment and resignation are expressed indirectly.

examples.title: Clash of Want (external desire) and Need (internal lack)
body: Condition: An ambitious young lawyer.
External goal (Want): To win every case by any means in order to become a partner at a major law firm.
Internal need (Need): To regain justice and conscience by not turning away from the tears of wronged victims.
Climax: When the opportunity arrives to fabricate evidence in order to win, the lawyer gives up Want and chooses Need, loses the case, and is reborn as a human being.
Interpretation: The character's true moral growth arc (character arc) is completed.

tf-10.title: Acting and Direction I: Konstantin Stanislavski and Realist Acting
explain: Acting before the nineteenth century remained at a 'melodramatic stylization,' in which emotions were imitated outwardly through exaggerated gestures and oratorical delivery. The person who overturned this and laid the scientific foundation for realist acting, acting that lives and breathes on stage without pretense, was **Konstantin Stanislavski** (1863–1938) of the Moscow Art Theatre in Russia.

The core principles of the Stanislavski System:
1. **Given circumstances**: Thoroughly grasp all the objective conditions in which the character finds themselves, including the time and place specified in the script, the weather, the character's social class, past history, and the events immediately before the scene.
2. **Magic 'if'**: The moment the actor entertains the assumption, "If I were actually in this tragic situation, how would I behave?", the defense mechanisms of reason are released, and the doors to unconscious imagination and genuine emotion open.
3. **Emotional memory**: An inner psychological technique that revives the sensory memories (the five senses) of sorrow, anger, and joy that the actor experienced in their own real life, and resonates them with the character's emotions. It was later developed in America by Lee Strasberg into 'method acting.'
4. **Method of physical action**: In his later years, Stanislavski, wary of the danger of forcing emotion, concentrated on concrete **physical actions**. Rather than trying hard to grieve, one immerses oneself in a concrete physical action, such as 'picking up a broken glass with trembling hands.' The principle of psychophysical unity holds that real emotion then follows naturally.

Communion and the circle of attention: The actor must draw a closed 'circle of attention,' concentrating only on themselves, the other actors, and the props on stage, without being conscious of the audience in the seats. When one responds in real time to the other actor's eyes and breathing, a living communion flows across the stage.

Limitation: Immersing oneself extremely in emotional memory can wear down the actor's actual mental health. Moreover, as Brecht pointed out, it leaves the audience no room to view reality critically and drops them into sentimental hypnosis.

examples.title: Securing the truthfulness of emotion through the magic 'if'
body: Condition: Playing a character who is wrongly accused of murder and imprisoned.
Step 1: The actor has never actually been falsely accused of murder.
Step 2: The actor opens the door of imagination with the question, "What if I were abandoned by the family I love most and locked in a room where no one believes my innocence?"
Interpretation: The imagined assumption (magic if) draws out the actor's inner true fear and the breath of innocence.

body: Condition: A scene of despair upon receiving news of a breakup.

Step 2: Search the coat pocket with trembling fingers for the car key and try to fit it into the keyhole, but keep missing. Carry out this concrete physical action.
Interpretation: The precise performance of a physical action triggers natural sorrow and frustration in both the actor and the audience.

tf-11.title: Acting and Direction II: Bertolt Brecht and Epic Theater
explain: Where Stanislavski completely immersed the audience in the reality on stage, moving them to tears and laughter, the German playwright and director **Bertolt Brecht** (1898–1956) made the opposite declaration: "The audience who enters the theater must not be made to leave behind their critical reason, just as they leave their coat and hat at the door!"

Brecht defined traditional Aristotelian theater (emotional immersion, catharsis, submission to fate) as the 'opiate of the bourgeois class,' and founded **epic theater**, which turns the audience into awake, critical observers.
- **Traditional drama**: Draws the audience into the events and exhausts their emotions ("I feel just as sad as that person. The world is simply like that.").
- **Epic theater**: Pushes the audience outside the events and makes them think critically about social structures ("Why must that character become so miserable? How should the social system be changed?").

The key device of Brecht's direction that realizes this critical distance is the **alienation effect** (Verfremdungseffekt). It is a technique that makes a reality taken for granted look strange, so that the audience begins to question it.
- **Exposed stage**: Lighting equipment, sound gear, and the backstage are left visible to the audience, constantly reminding them that "this place is not reality, but only a play."
- **Narrator and placards**: Captions or signs announce the outcome of the events before the act begins, so that the audience focuses not on 'how will it end?' but on 'why does it end this way?', the social causality.
- **Music and songs (chorus)**: When emotion rises, a cheerful song or a satirical chorus is inserted out of nowhere, coolly breaking emotional immersion.

**Gestus**: In Brecht's acting, the actor does not become one with the character and weep. Instead, the actor takes the stance of objectively 'showing' the audience a social attitude and gesture (gestus) that condenses the character's social class relations and contradictions.

Limitation: Extreme alienation can tire the audience, making them feel like students sitting through a dull lecture on sociology. True Brechtian direction leads the audience to revolutionary thought not through cold cynicism, but when it is accompanied by cheerful satire, humor, and intellectual play.

examples.title: Comparing audience responses to traditional drama and epic theater
body: Traditional drama audience: "Yes, I am in the same situation. Human life is an unavoidable tragedy... (tears and catharsis, acceptance of reality)"

Epic theater audience: "How shocking! That is not normal. Why does this society allow such a law? When I leave the theater, I must reform that law! (critical awakening and the will for social change)"
Interpretation: It is an opposition between catharsis, which stitches reality back together, and social change through alienation.

examples.title: Example of applying the alienation technique in direction
body: Condition: A sad scene in which the protagonist is dragged miserably to the execution ground.
Step 1: In traditional direction, a sad minor-key score and dark lighting would be used to induce tears.

Step 2: A Brechtian production turns on white fluorescent lights as bright as midday, projects the caption "Bankruptcy of the capitalist justice system" on a screen on stage, and the actor suddenly looks straight at the audience and sings a cheerful tango.
Interpretation: The audience is made to stop weeping and to coolly gaze at the absurdity of the justice system that drove the protagonist to death.

tf-12.title: Acting and Direction III: Nine-Area Stage Blocking and the Power of Gaze
explain: Within the limited physical rectangle of the theater stage, where actors stand, where they walk, and whom they look at is not simply traffic control. An actor's position and movement path are themselves a language of **stage blocking** that visually translates power, psychological closeness, and the weight of emotion between characters.

explain.alt: Floor plan of the nine-area blocking grid of a proscenium stage. The audience seating is at the bottom. The stage is divided into nine parts: upstage at the top (UR, UC, UL), center stage in the middle (CR, CS, CL), and downstage at the bottom (DR, DC, DL). Left and right are defined from the point of view of the actor on stage: the actor's right is stage right (R), and the actor's left is stage left (L).

explain:
1. **Names of the nine areas and the reference for direction**:
Stage left and stage right are always defined **from the point of view of the actor on stage looking out at the audience**. From the audience's position, the left side is the actor's right, so it is called **stage right** (SR). The audience's right is the actor's left, so it is called **stage left** (SL).
- **Downstage (front)**: The area of the stage closest to the audience. It got its name because the stage was formerly raked, sloping down toward the audience. Emotional closeness with the audience is maximized here, and the delivery of lines and charisma are strongest.
- **Upstage (back)**: The deep rear of the stage. Distance from the audience increases, giving a sense of separation, isolation, or transcendent authority and mystery.
- **Center stage (middle)**: The exact center of the stage (CS) and down center (DC) are the core of power, holding the strongest visual weight.

2. **Psychological power dynamics of blocking**:
- **Level**: The vertical height difference between a standing person, a kneeling person, and a person standing on a staircase immediately imprints a power relation of domination and submission.
- **Triangulation**: When three or more characters are present, attention automatically concentrates on the character standing at the apex of the triangle.
- **Upstaging**: When one actor deliberately retreats upstage (backward) of another, the actor in front must turn their back to the audience to look back, so the upstage actor monopolizes the gaze. In acting jargon, this is the act of taking attention away from others.

3. **Meaning of entrance and exit paths**: In the Western theater tradition, stage right was historically used as the formal and authoritative entrance and exit, while stage left was often used for the paths of worldly or threatening characters.

Limitation: Blocking based on the proscenium arch (picture-frame stage) does not work on thrust stages, where the audience surrounds three or four sides, or in arena (circular) theaters. On a circular stage, actors inevitably turn their backs to half of the audience, so a dynamic spiral of rotating movement becomes essential.

examples.title: Downstage center (DC) blocking for a soliloquy scene
body: Condition: Hamlet agonizes over "To be or not to be" in a soliloquy.
Step 1: The king and courtiers at the back of the stage (upstage) are frozen in darkness.
Step 2: Hamlet slowly walks out to downstage center (DC), right at the edge of the audience, and murmurs while gazing into the audience's eyes.
Interpretation: By narrowing the distance to the audience, it completes an emotional bond in which Hamlet directly confesses his most secret inner pain to the audience.

body: Condition: An interrogation scene between a ruler and a prisoner.
Step 1: At first, the ruler sits on the throne at the top of the stairs (high level), and the prisoner lies prostrate on the floor (low level).
Step 2: The prisoner exposes the ruler's foul secret, slowly rises, and strides up the stairs, while the shocked ruler staggers from the throne and sinks down at the foot of the stairs.
Interpretation: Through the reversal of physical vertical levels, a power reversal more overwhelming than the dialogue is imprinted visually.

tf-13.title: Film Mise-en-scène and Cinematography I: Framing, Depth of Field, and Deep Focus
explain: What to include in the rectangular frame through the camera lens, and what to leave out? **Mise-en-scène** (a French term meaning 'placing on stage') refers to the overall harmony of the people, sets, lighting, costumes, and camera angle placed within the film frame.

1. **Shot size and emotional distance**:
- **Extreme long shot (ELS)**: Shows vast nature or an entire city, revealing human smallness or isolation.
- **Full shot (FS)**: Captures the whole body from head to toe, catching action within the environment.
- **Medium shot (MS)**: Frames the upper body from the waist up and forms the standard distance of everyday conversation.
- **Close-up (CU)**: Fills the frame with the whole face, transferring the depth of emotion in subtle glances and expressions to the audience.

2. **Camera lens and depth of field**:
- **Focal length**: A standard 50 mm lens is similar to human vision. A **wide-angle lens** (28 mm or less) has a wide angle of view and exaggerated perspective, so the foreground looks huge and the background recedes, creating a dynamic distortion. A **telephoto lens** (85 mm or more) compresses the background, making the distance between front and back look close.
- **Shallow focus**: An out-of-focus technique in which only the character is sharp and the background is softly blurred, isolating the subject from its surroundings and monopolizing the gaze (aperture open at f/1.4 to 2.8).
- **Deep focus**: A technique in which the entire frame, from the foreground character to the distant background, is sharply in focus (aperture stopped down to f/11 to 22, with a wide-angle lens and high-intensity lighting required).

3. **André Bazin and deep-focus realism**:
The French film critic André Bazin praised the deep focus achieved in Orson Welles's <Citizen Kane> (1941, cinematographer Gregg Toland). Rather than forcibly shaping the audience's gaze through editing (montage), showing several layers of events at once within a single frame gives **"the democratic freedom of the gaze, in which the audience can choose for themselves where in the image to look"**. Bazin saw this as the summit of realism, in which film preserved the temporality and spatial unity of reality.

Limitation: Deep focus technically demands an enormous amount of light and a narrow aperture, which exhausts actors and crew. It also carries the directorial risk that the audience's gaze scatters and they miss an important dramatic moment.

examples.title: Analysis of deep-focus mise-en-scène in the film 'Citizen Kane'
body: Condition: The scene in which Kane's early childhood adoption contract is signed.
Step 1: In the foreground, the cold face of the mother signing the adoption papers is sharply captured.

Step 2: In the middle ground, the father stands helplessly protesting, and through the window in the far background, young Kane, unaware of anything, is sledding in the snow, all visible at once in perfect focus.
Interpretation: Because three layers of space coexist in one frame without editing, the tragedy of a child's fate being sold into the hands of adults is maximized.

examples.title: The spatial compression effect of a telephoto lens
body: Condition: The protagonist flees from a sniper, sprinting at full speed toward the camera.
Step 1: Shoot with a 200 mm telephoto lens.
Step 2: The space between the background and the protagonist is compressed flat, creating a nightmarish sense of exhaustion in which, however hard they run, they seem to be running in place.
Interpretation: The optical properties of the lens convert the character's psychological despair into visual form.

tf-14.title: Film Mise-en-scène and Cinematography II: Three-Point Lighting Design and Lighting Style
explain: Film is 'writing with light' (cinematography). Lighting is not merely the electrical technology of brightening dark places. It is the core of mise-en-scène, shaping the volume of the subject, suggesting the psychological state of the characters, and determining the genre tone of the whole film. The basic framework of character lighting established since classical Hollywood is **three-point lighting**.

explain.alt: Floor plan of a three-point lighting layout for filming a person. The actor is at the center, and the camera is positioned below. At 45 degrees to the front left is the key light (main light, 100%). At 45 degrees to the front right is the fill light (secondary light, 50%). At the rear right is the back light (rim light separating the subject from the background). Arrows show the light being aimed at the actor.

explain:
Let us break down the three main light sources of three-point lighting and their roles.
1. **Key light (main light)**: The strongest light (100%), shining diagonally from above the actor's face at 30 to 45 degrees. It forms the character's shape, three-dimensionality, and main shadows, becoming the dominant light source of the scene.
2. **Fill light (secondary light)**: Placed 45 degrees in front, on the opposite side from the key light, with its intensity set softly at 25 to 50% of the key light. It gently brings out the detail in the deep shadows created by the key light, adjusting the **lighting ratio** (contrast).
3. **Back light (backlight / rim light)**: Shines from high behind the actor onto the shoulders and hair. It creates a dazzling edge of light (rim light) around the character's outline, separating the character visually from the dark background and giving a sense of three-dimensional depth.

Lighting styles and the differentiation of genres:
- **High-key lighting**: Raises the fill light to reduce the lighting ratio extremely, to 1:1 to 2:1. A bright, airy image with almost no shadows, used in romantic comedies and family musicals.
- **Low-key lighting**: Turns off or greatly reduces the fill light, raising the lighting ratio to 8:1 to 16:1 or more. It creates a sharp contrast between pitch-black shadows and harsh light, visualizing the anxiety and corruption of film noir, crime thrillers, and horror.

Rembrandt lighting: A classical technique in which the key light is aimed from the side at 45 degrees, leaving a triangle of light on the shadowed cheek. It gives the character a sense of deep anguish and intellectual three-dimensionality.

Limitation: Artificial three-point lighting is perfect for studio shooting, but in contemporary documentaries and neorealist films it can look too affected and contrived. Contemporary cinematographers often prefer naturalistic lighting that imitates 'practical light' (light sources that actually exist in the scene), such as real window light or lamps on location.

examples.title: Low-key lighting direction in film noir
body: Condition: A private detective waits for a culprit in a night office.
Step 1: Thrust the key light strongly through the gaps in the blind slats, casting a striped shadow across the detective's face.
Step 2: Completely cut off the fill light, sinking half of the face into pitch-black darkness (shadow).
Interpretation: Through the extreme division of light and dark, the detective's moral wandering and the corruption of the criminal city are completed visually.

examples.title: Separation effect of the back light (rim light)
body: Condition: An actor in a black suit walks down a dark night alley.
Step 1: Without the back light, the black clothes sink into the dark background, and only the neck seems to float.
Step 2: Shine a back light from 45 degrees above and behind the actor, giving the shoulder line and the brim of the hat a thin silver edge of light.
Interpretation: The dark background and dark costume separate, and the character's silhouette comes fully alive in the space.

tf-15.title: Film Mise-en-scène and Cinematography III: Camera Movement and the Aesthetics of the Long Take
explain: The camera does not stay fixed on a tripod; it becomes a living human gaze that explores space. Camera movement is a powerful aesthetic engine that turns the audience from passive spectators of events into 'invisible companions.'

1. **Technical grammar of camera movement**:
- **Pan**: The camera body stays fixed while the lens turns horizontally, left and right, like turning the head.
- **Tilt**: The lens sweeps vertically, up and down (for example, tilting up from the base of a building to its top).
- **Tracking / dolly**: The camera is mounted on rails or a wheeled dolly and moves directly through space, forward, backward, and sideways, following the subject.
- **Crane / jib**: The camera is hung from a large mechanical arm and rises three-dimensionally from the ground into the air in a grand movement.
- **Steadicam**: A special spring vest worn by the camera operator produces a smooth, floating gaze free of shaking, even while climbing stairs or walking down a narrow alley.

2. **Dolly zoom (vertigo effect)**:
This is a technique first developed in Alfred Hitchcock's <Vertigo>. The camera moves toward the subject (dolly-in) while the lens simultaneously zooms out, or conversely moves backward while zooming in. The size of the central character remains unchanged in the frame, but the perspective of the background is unrealistically distorted, so the space seems to stretch or warp. It is a supreme visual effect for expressing the moment a character experiences extreme psychological panic or shock.

3. **Long take and sequence shot**:
A technique in which an entire scene is captured in a single, continuous shot without cutting in editing, lasting one minute or more, and at most several to around ten minutes. (Examples: Orson Welles's <Touch of Evil> and Alfonso Cuarón's <Children of Men>.)
The long take preserves the temporality of reality and the continuity of space without cutting. It gives both the performing actors and the audience an extreme sense of real-time suspense, and proves a live, on-site realism in which artificial manipulation is impossible.

Limitation: A long take carries enormous production cost and risk. A mistake of even one second, a stumble in an actor's line, or a lighting timing error can require the whole take to be shot again from the beginning. Moreover, a long take that shows off technical virtuosity without a clear dramatic motivation for the movement can become a poison that bores the audience.

examples.title: Geometric principle of the dolly zoom
body: Condition: A close-up moment in which a character realizes a shocking truth.
Step 1: The dolly camera moves forward (dolly-in) toward the character's face.
Step 2: At the same time, the focal length zooms out toward a wide angle, keeping the size of the character's face exactly constant.
Interpretation: With the character fixed, only the background space recedes far behind, completing the vertigo illusion of the ground giving way underfoot.

Step 1: Without cutting, a special camera that rotates 360 degrees inside the car films the scene in one take for four minutes.
Step 2: The entire process, from firebombs flying in to gunfire breaking out, unfolds in real time before the audience's eyes.
Interpretation: The inevitability of being unable to rely on editing plunges the audience into overwhelming terror, as if they were trapped together in the back seat of the car.

tf-16.title: Editing and Montage I: Classical Continuity Editing and the 180-Degree Rule
explain: Joining hundreds of fragmentary recorded shots into one smooth film is called editing. In the early twentieth century, Hollywood established a transparent editing grammar, **classical continuity editing** (also called invisible editing), which keeps the audience from noticing, while they watch, that the film is an arrangement of cut-together images.

The great principle of continuity editing is to maintain the continuity of time and space.
- **Match cut**:
  - **Match on action**: Connects a long shot of a person turning a doorknob with a close-up of the door opening and the person entering, at the middle of the movement, creating uninterrupted motion.
  - **Eyeline match**: After a shot of a person looking to the right, shows the object of that gaze, so that the direction of the eyes matches.
  - **Shot-reverse-shot**: When alternately showing two people in conversation, cuts between over-the-shoulder angles in a regular rhythm.

explain.alt: Diagram of the classical continuity editing 180-degree rule. A horizontal dotted imaginary line (action line) is drawn between character A and character B. Camera 1 and camera 2, positioned within the 180-degree half-circle arc below the imaginary line, are the permitted shooting zone. Camera X, which has crossed over the imaginary line to the upper side, is marked in red; it is a violating camera that crosses the line and reverses the gaze.

explain:
The most sacred and inviolable absolute rule of continuity editing is the **180-degree rule** (180-Degree Rule / Axis of Action). Let us examine the diagram above closely.
When two characters, A and B, face each other and converse, an imaginary straight line forms connecting their eyes. This is called the **action line (imaginary line)**. The camera must remain within the 180-degree half-circle on one side of this line.
- **Cameras 1 and 2**: Positioned side by side below the imaginary line. From camera 1, character A stands on the left of the frame looking right; from camera 2, character B stands on the right of the frame looking left. When the two shots are joined, the two people's gazes meet naturally at the center of the frame.
- **Camera X (violating the imaginary line)**: If the camera leaps over the imaginary line to the opposite side, characters A and B are both distorted into looking in the same direction (frame right). The audience's spatial perception collapses, not knowing whether the two are facing each other or turned away from each other (a reverse cut error).

Limitation: Strictly observing the 180-degree rule avoids spatial confusion, but the narrative can become overly exemplary and flat. In <Breathless> (1960), the French New Wave director Jean-Luc Godard deliberately crossed the 180-degree line and fired off **jump cuts** that skipped the flow of time, shattering the illusionism of classical film.

examples.title: Editing a dialogue scene that observes the 180-degree axis

Step 1: Two cameras are placed below the imaginary line connecting the two people, and shoot.
Step 2: The detective's shot (gazing from left to right) and the suspect's shot (gazing from right to left) are cross-cut.
Interpretation: The audience clearly perceives that the two characters sit facing each other in one space, locked in a tense staring contest.

body: Condition: For directorial intent, the camera must be moved to the opposite side of the imaginary line.
Step 1: Do not cut immediately after skipping over the line.
Step 2: Insert a single neutral shot passing in front of the two characters, or show a continuous tracking shot in which the camera smoothly crosses the imaginary line.
Interpretation: By showing the audience the visual process of the transition, a new axis is formed without causing spatial dizziness.

tf-17.title: Editing and Montage II: Soviet Montage and Eisenstein's Theory of Collision
explain: While Hollywood clung to 'transparent continuity' that hides the existence of editing, the young filmmakers of revolutionary Soviet Russia in the 1920s set off a radical theory: **"the essential nature of the art of film lies solely in editing (montage)"**. The discovery was that when two different shots collide, a completely new third meaning, which did not exist in either film strip, is born in the audience's mind.

1. **Kuleshov Effect**:
Lev Kuleshov took one close-up shot of a famous actor's expressionless face and carried out a legendary experiment, combining it with three different shots and showing them to the audience.
- [expressionless face] + [a bowl of hot soup] $\rightarrow$ Audience: "The actor is feeling hunger!"
- [expressionless face] + [a child lying in a coffin] $\rightarrow$ Audience: "The actor is sunk in bitter grief!"
- [expressionless face] + [a seductive woman lying on a sofa] $\rightarrow$ Audience: "The actor harbors burning desire!"
The actor's expression was exactly the same piece of film, yet the audience actively synthesized emotion from the juxtaposition of the shots placed before and after it. This proves the basic montage principle: the meaning of a shot is determined not by the content of the shot itself, but by **'its combination with other shots'**.

explain.alt: Diagram of Eisenstein's dialectical collision montage. On the left, shot A (thesis: a demonstration of hungry workers) and on the right, shot B (antithesis: an ox being slaughtered in a slaughterhouse) collide, deriving a new synthetic concept C below (synthesis: the brutality of the massacre of the people by capitalist power), forming a triangular dialectical structure.

explain:
2. **Sergei Eisenstein's dialectical collision montage**:
Eisenstein transplanted the dialectic of Hegel and Marx (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) into film editing. As in the diagram above, when 'thesis (shot A)' and 'antithesis (shot B)' collide violently on screen, a third, abstract concept, the **'synthesis' (concept C)**, flashes into the audience's mind like lightning. A representative example is <Strike>, in which the gunshots suppressing workers and a bull having its throat cut in a slaughterhouse are cross-collided to explode the intellectual concept of 'the massacre of the people by capitalist power'.

Eisenstein's five layers of montage:
1. **Metric montage**: The beat rhythm according to the physical length of the shots.
2. **Rhythmic montage**: The collision of the direction and tempo of movement within shots (the Odessa Steps scene in <Battleship Potemkin>).
3. **Tonal montage**: The collision of light-dark tones or emotional moods.
4. **Overtone montage**: The composite sum of metric, rhythmic, and tonal montage.
5. **Intellectual montage (Intellectual Montage)**: The highest layer, which injects advanced philosophical and political metaphors through visual collision.

Limitation: Intellectual montage easily degenerates into a propaganda tool that imposes the author's ideology on the audience in one direction, and it has been criticized for limiting the audience's autonomous interpretation.

examples.title: Analysis of the Odessa Steps scene in the film 'Battleship Potemkin'
body: Condition: The Tsar's army descends the steps, massacring the people.
Step 1: A mechanical rhythmic shot of the army marching down, stomping in boot-beat (downward motion).
Step 2: A close-up shot of a mother, bleeding and screaming upward for her son to be saved (upward motion).
Step 3: A shot of a baby tumbling down the steps after the pram is lost, and a shot of a woman whose glasses are broken, are hammered together in quick beats (rhythm).
Interpretation: The combination of opposing directions of movement and shortened shot lengths completes one of the most intense montages of terror and anger in film history.

body: Condition: The aim is to criticize the vanity of Kerensky, head of the provisional government.
Step 1: Show a shot of Kerensky proudly puffing out his chest.
Step 2: In the next shot, join a mechanical sculpture of a peacock spreading its wings wide and showing off.
Interpretation: The collision of two dissimilar shots produces the critical concept (intellectual meaning) that 'Kerensky is an incompetent leader, vain like a peacock.'

tf-18.title: Film Sound Aesthetics: Diegetic and Non-Diegetic Sound and Sound Design
explain: Since the era of the talkie opened with <The Jazz Singer> in 1927, sound has ceased to be background noise that merely supports the image and has become an equal aesthetic axis that defines the space and time of a film. The French sound theorist Michel Chion defined the phenomenon in which, when image and sound meet, an entirely new third value arises rather than 1 + 1 = 2, as **'added value'**.

1. **Diegetic versus non-diegetic sound**:
- **Diegetic sound (in-story sound)**: Sound whose source lies within the fictional world of the film (the diegesis). The characters in the film can actually hear it. Examples include a character's dialogue, the sound of rain, the sound of a door closing, and a song playing from a radio within the story.
- **Non-diegetic sound (out-of-story sound)**: Sound artificially added from outside the world of the film. The characters in the film cannot hear it; only the audience does. This includes the film's background music (score, BGM), narration (voice-over), and sound effects that heighten tension.
- **Crossing the boundary**: Contemporary films deliberately blur this boundary. For example, a radio song heard by a character (diegetic) expands into a grand orchestral background score (non-diegetic) as the scene changes.

2. **The four main components of film sound**:
- **Dialogue**: The core information that conveys the narrative and the subtext.
- **Sound effects (SFX)**: Door sounds, gunshots, car engine noise, and so on.
- **Foley**: Post-synchronized sound recorded in a studio, in which a Foley artist snaps celery to produce the sound of breaking bones, or walks in shoes over a gravel tray to perform and record a character's footsteps directly.
- **Ambience / room tone**: The background sound of a space (the sound of wind, the murmur of a city, the faint resonance of air in an empty room). Without it, the image seems to die, as if trapped in a vacuum tube.

3. **Sound bridge**:
A technique in which the picture still remains in the previous scene while the sound of the next scene is heard in advance (L-cut), or the picture has moved to the next scene while the dialogue or sound of the previous scene continues (J-cut). It is a highly skilled editing technique that smoothly stitches the visual sense of discontinuity between scenes with the continuity of sound.

Limitation: Overuse of background music can become a sentimental imposition that prevents the audience from focusing on the character's silence and expressions. Sometimes, perfect **silence** delivers an emotional shock hundreds of times stronger than a thunderous roar.

Step 1: The sound of the piano keys being struck is diegetic sound, because the characters are also hearing it.

Step 2: As the music flows, the scene transitions to a montage of the pianist's childhood memories. The piano sound expands its function into a tender background score (non-diegetic) that wraps the flashback scene.
Interpretation: Through the shift in the hierarchy of sound, the past and the present are emotionally stitched together as one.

Interpretation: The sound bridge strongly binds two dissimilar times and spaces psychologically.

Film achieves both on-site realism and the heightening of a character's psychological emotion by organically combining and crossing these two kinds of sound.

tf-19.title: Capstone: Scenario Analysis and Comprehensive Continuity Shooting and Editing
explain: The culmination of the bachelor's program in film and theater is to apply everything learned so far, **dramaturgy (three-act structure, super-objective, subtext), acting and direction (blocking, Brecht), camera mise-en-scène (three-point lighting, depth of field), and editing montage with the 180-degree imaginary line and sound design**, comprehensively to one scene of an actual film script, completing a finished directorial continuity.

Let us analyze comprehensively a scene from a fictional short film (Scene #12: the old interrogation room).
1. **Narrative and dramatic analysis**: This is a crisis scene just before the climax in the late second act. The veteran detective Suhyeon's external goal (Want) is to extract a confession within 24 hours, but his internal lack (Need) is to face his own past mistakes. The subtext behind the suspect Jinu's surface line ("This coffee is really warm") is "I have your weakness in my hands." The psychological initiative of the two characters reverses through three beats.
2. **Shooting and mise-en-scène design**: Use a 35 mm wide-angle lens to intensify the claustrophobia of the interrogation room's walls. The lighting uses a single fluorescent light over the interrogation table as the key light and extremely suppresses the fill light, establishing the contrast of darkness in a **low-key** style. A tormented triangle of Rembrandt light falls on the detective's face.
3. **180-degree axis and continuity**: Set the axis of action (axis of action) of the gazes of the two people across the table, and place all cameras only on the west side of the axis (the side toward the door). The detective's over-the-shoulder shot (looking right) and the suspect's reverse shot (looking left) achieve a perfect match of gaze.
4. **Sound design**: Lay the buzz of the fluorescent light and the second hand of the wall clock as diegetic ambience to make the pressure of time visible, and place a silence technique, in which the sound of the second hand is erased in a single stroke at the moment of psychological crack.

The core of comprehensive direction is whether all formal elements are aligned toward a single **thematic unity** (Unity). Lighting, camera movement, and sound must be perfectly synchronized with the conflict structure of the script.

examples.title: Designing beats and camera angles for Scene #12
body: Beat 1 (the detective's pressure): The detective stands and looks down; a high angle (the detective's power).
Beat 2 (the suspect's counterattack): The suspect points out a contradiction in the key evidence; a low angle (overturning of power).
Beat 3 (deadlock of silence): The two people's eyes meet in a tight close-up shot-reverse-shot cross-cut.
Interpretation: Changes in the power dynamics between the characters are precisely translated through the height of the camera angle (level) and the shot sizes.

examples.title: Verifying the reverse-cut error when crossing the axis (Reverse Cut)
body: Condition: The detective becomes agitated and starts walking around the table.
Step 1: The camera follows the detective's path of movement, rotating along on a rail dolly to naturally track the imaginary line.
Step 2: When the detective stands behind the suspect, a new 180-degree axis is established, so smooth gaze continuity is maintained without a jump cut.
Interpretation: Continuity editing is preserved through the dynamic renewal of the imaginary line to fit the moving character.

checks.prompt: When shooting the table dialogue scene in which the detective and the suspect sit facing each other in the interrogation room, what iron rule must the crew follow to prevent the error of inconsistent gaze direction (reverse cut)?
checks.hint: The principle of keeping to one side of the 180-degree imaginary line.
checks.explanation: Camera positions must be taken only within one 180-degree area of the imaginary line for the direction of gaze to be preserved.
options: Place all cameras only on one side of the 180-degree imaginary line (action line) connecting the two characters' eyes
Shoot all shots only from the top of the ceiling
Have the actors deliver their lines with their eyes closed
Place the camera at the exact center of the table and keep rotating it 360 degrees

checks.prompt: Which lighting style minimizes the fill light and maximizes contrast to visualize the eerie suspense and psychological unease of the interrogation room?
checks.hint: The low-key style, in which darkness dominates.
checks.explanation: Low-key lighting, which creates deep shadows and high contrast, suits the thriller's interrogation room.

checks.prompt: In analyzing the subtext of the scene: a character outwardly says an ordinary line, "The weather is really cold today," but inwardly carries the intention of a threat, "I know the secret you are hiding." What is the essence of this line?
checks.hint: The intention hidden behind the line (subtext).
checks.explanation: This is the typical subtext, formed by the gap between the surface line and the inner meaning.
options: Dramatic tension formed through the gap between the line (text) and the subtext
A failure to memorize the script

checks.prompt: At the moment the tense psychological suspense in the interrogation room reaches its peak, what sound design technique, and what effect, cuts off all clock-second-hand sounds and mechanical sounds in an instant?
checks.hint: The deliberate aesthetic use of silence.
checks.explanation: Perfect silence focuses the audience's auditory attention and creates extreme psychological suspense.
options: Silence technique that maximizes psychological pressure and auditory shock
An infinite loop of diegetic sound

tf-20.title: Capstone: Short Film Directorial Plan and Continuity Design
explain: The final capstone task of the bachelor's program in film and theater is to write, and critically review, a **'directorial plan (Director's Statement) and storyboard continuity design'** for one fictional short film. The goal is to turn the ideas in one's head into a professional filmmaking language that the crew on set (camera, lighting, art, sound, and actors) can communicate about without error.

The standard seven-part framework of a directorial plan is as follows.
1. **Logline and planning intent**: A clear one- or two-sentence logline, the director's intent, and the theme of the era posed to the audience
2. **Character and narrative analysis**: Plot turning points within the three-act structure, the protagonist's super-objective and Want vs. Need conflict, and the subtext of key scenes
3. **Visual concept and mise-en-scène**: Key color and color palette, set space design, and the lens focal length and depth-of-field strategy
4. **Lighting and look design**: Three-point lighting layout, high-key/low-key contrast, and the synchronized light source settings of the key light
5. **Storyboard continuity**: Shot list of three key scenes, shot size, camera angle, whether the 180-degree axis is observed, and camera movement (dolly / pan / handheld)
6. **Sound design plan**: Diegetic environmental sound (ambience), the score that leads the character's emotional line (non-diegetic), and the design of Foley and sound bridges
7. **Critical self-evaluation**: The originality of the directorial plan, expected production risks, and plan B alternatives for technical weaknesses

A superb directorial plan has every formal element **precisely synchronized with the protagonist's inner psychology**. At moments of sorrow, the lighting sinks into low-key; at moments of isolation, the distortion of a wide-angle lens intervenes; at moments of awakening, silence and sound bridges must burst out.

In the self-evaluation, three things must be asked severely. (1) Did my direction avoid falling into cliché (conventional triteness) and pioneer an original visual language? (2) Are there no errors in the visual grammar of continuity, such as the 180-degree axis or the eyeline match? (3) Is the design feasible enough to withstand the physical constraints of the set (time, lighting, budget)?

Limitation: This capstone task is not auto-graded. Based on the checklist provided, the learner reviews and supplements their own directorial plan strictly and self-directedly, from a film director's point of view.

examples.title: Example opening summary of a short film directorial plan
body: Work title: <When the Trigger Is Pulled> (running time 15 minutes, psychological drama).

Logline: A detective nearing retirement faces an existential crossroads when a boy he once falsely framed comes looking for him as an adult: will he conceal his own crime, or reveal the truth in court?

Directorial concept: Strictly observing the 180-degree axis in a narrow apartment living room, with a 35 mm wide-angle lens, deep focus, and low-key Rembrandt lighting, the film coldly captures the inescapable moral judgment of the two characters.
Interpretation: A cinematic opening in which the narrative and the visual concept are perfectly combined.

examples.title: Example of a continuity self-check
body: Condition: Reviewing the storyboard of Scene #5.
Step 1: A reverse-cut error is found, in which the camera crosses the imaginary line when moving from shot 3 to shot 4.
Step 2: Revised by inserting a frontal master shot of the two people in between as an insert shot, so that the axis of gaze is crossed naturally.
Interpretation: A case in which a continuity error was caught in advance and corrected with the grammar of direction.

checks.prompt: Arrange in order the procedure for producing a short film directorial plan and storyboard.
checks.hint: Narrative analysis → visual and lighting concept → shot list and imaginary line → storyboard and sound → self-check.
checks.explanation: Starting from the analysis of the scenario, the work is completed through mise-en-scène, continuity, sound, and directorial critique.
items: Confirm the logline and analyze the narrative and character arc of the three-act structure
Design the visual mise-en-scène concept, three-point lighting, and color look
Write the shot list for each scene and verify the 180-degree imaginary line
Sketch the storyboard and specify camera movement and sound design
Critically self-evaluate the originality of the directorial plan and its feasibility on set

checks.prompt: During storyboard continuity review, an error was found in which shot 3 (looking right) and shot 4 (looking right) are joined, so the two people's gazes deviate in the same direction. What is the most correct directorial remedy?
checks.hint: Observe the 180-degree imaginary line, or insert a neutral shot.
checks.explanation: Gaze alignment is preserved only by keeping to one side of the axis, or by passing through a neutral shot.
options: Reposition the camera angles so as not to cross the 180-degree imaginary line, or insert a frontal neutral shot in between to align the axis of gaze
Flip the screen upside down so that it is viewed upside down
Handle all dialogue with subtitles only

checks.prompt: Summarize the core directorial plan of the fictional short film you will direct in three to five sentences. Include the logline, the turning points of the three-act narrative, the lighting and mise-en-scène concept, and the 180-degree imaginary line and sound plan.
checks.hint: Compress frames 1 to 7 into one sentence each, with key words.
checks.explanation: The logline, the narrative structure, the lighting of the mise-en-scène, and the imaginary-line sound must combine harmoniously.
checks.model: The short film <The Interrogation of Light and Shadow> is a psychological drama about a detective and a prisoner trying to conceal a past truth, following a three-act narrative structure in which the decisive secret is exposed at the midpoint. The interrogation room is visualized with a 35 mm wide-angle lens and low-key three-point lighting, showing the characters' moral split. The table dialogue scene strictly follows the 180-degree rule to secure the match of gaze, and maximizes suspense through the tense silence and the diegetic sound of the clock's second hand.

checks.prompt: Final capstone task: Write a short film directorial plan and storyboard continuity design. Include all seven frames (logline and planning intent; character and three-act narrative analysis; visual concept and lens mise-en-scène; three-point lighting design; storyboard shot list and 180-degree imaginary line verification; sound design; critical self-evaluation), each under its own subheading, and complete it at 400 characters or more.
checks.hint: Divide the seven frames into subheadings and write in the professional format of a film director's plan.
checks.explanation: This task is not auto-graded. Check your own directorial plan yourself with the checklist.
checklist: Wrote a clear logline and directorial intent
Analyzed the protagonist's super-objective and the turning points of the three-act structure
Designed the lens angle of view, depth of field, and three-point lighting look
Described the shot list and the continuity that observes the 180-degree imaginary line
Specified diegetic and non-diegetic sound and the direction of silence
Completed the critical self-check on the originality of the direction and its feasibility on set
